title: Agentic Neural Architecture Search
claim: A three-stage pipeline lets an LLM design a seed and slotted search space that conventional search then optimizes.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed arrows linking phases, colored phase banners
description: A wide three-panel figure showing the AgentNAS pipeline from left to right. Each panel has a colored title banner: green for Phase 1 (LLM-driven Seed Search), blue for Phase 2 (Search Space Synthesis), purple for Phase 3 (Neural Architecture Search). Phase 1 shows an LLM Architecture Planner box branching into Summary, Experiment, Explore and Stop actions. Code Generator robots feed a leaderboard table, with a dashed loop returning to the planner. Phase 2 has four input icons (seed architecture, training recipe, data exploration report, last results summary) feeding an LLM Slot Planner. The planner outputs slot columns with Seed and LLM-proposed alternative modules in blue, orange and red. Phase 3 shows rows of colored squares for random search, evolutionary search with mutations and parent labels, and DARTS with softmax blocks. Crown icons mark the best candidates.
caption: The AgentNAS pipeline. Phase 1: an LLM Planner repeatedly proposes architectures, which are implemented, trained under a proxy schedule, and added to a leaderboard. The Planner summarizes each round of results and continues until it stops improving, returning a seed architecture and its training recipe. Phase 2: the seed is decomposed into a slotted architecture with several alternatives per slot, which defines a task-specific search space. Phase 3: a conventional NAS algorithm explores this space. Each square represents one slot, and a full row of squares is one candidate architecture. The panel shows random search, regularized evolution, and differentiable search as examples.
abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) methods have grown increasingly efficient, but they still operate within manually designed search spaces that require domain expertise and must be rebuilt for each new task. Large language models (LLMs) can write architectures in an open-ended code space, yet it is unclear how the work should be divided between LLM-driven design and NAS-driven search. We propose a way to combine the two. An LLM first designs a seed architecture and then decomposes it into a slotted architecture: a scaffold with named, interchangeable module slots that defines a bounded, task-specific search space, which a conventional NAS algorithm then explores without any manual engineering. We implement this in AgentNAS, a three-phase pipeline whose phases can be evaluated separately. On 17 tasks from NAS-Bench-360 and Unseen NAS, covering classification, dense regression, segmentation, and multi-label tagging, AgentNAS outperforms published baselines, including task-specific expert designs, on 11 tasks. Extensive ablation studies show that LLMs find strong architectures quickly but soon plateau, and that switching to NAS at this point yields further gains, indicating that the two approaches are complementary. Experiments with five LLMs show that seed architecture design is effective across all of them, whereas constructing a usable search space requires a minimum level of model capability. Our code is available at https://github.com/alroimfebruary/AgentNAS.
